module.name: cli
module.spec: Run dispatches on args[0] to init, todo, reset, link, unlink, list, show, diff, help, skill, config, or version. No args, --help, -h, and help all print the help text with exit code 0. Unknown commands return an error message with help text and exit code 1. Missing args for reset/link/unlink/show/diff return a usage message with an example and exit code 1. Reset accepts 1 arg (a closure hash) plus optional --dry-run. Diff accepts 1 arg (a closure hash) or `--all`. Link and unlink accept marker+spec args plus optional --dry-run. Before any subcommand dispatches, the dispatch pipeline runs three uniform prechecks: (0) global_flag_stripping removes --json/--no-color/--color= from args (see global flags), (1) the help_flag check, and (2) the unknown_flag_rejection check. All run for every subcommand including those that take no arguments (init, todo, skill). The version command flows through dispatch like every other command (see version in dispatch).

For EVERY subcommand (init, todo, list, show, diff, link, unlink, reset, skill), if args[1] is --help or -h, the CLI prints that subcommand's usage text with exit code 0 and does NOT dispatch the subcommand. This check happens uniformly at the top of Run before the switch, so it works for subcommands that take no arguments (init, todo, skill) as well as those that take arguments. Each subcommand's usage text describes its syntax, purpose, and a short example. Top-level `drift` (no args), `drift help`, `drift --help`, and `drift -h` all print the main help text with exit code 0.

When any arg to a subcommand starts with `--` and is not a recognized flag for that subcommand, the CLI prints "unknown flag: --XYZ" with exit code 1 and does NOT dispatch the subcommand. This prevents silent misinterpretation where a mistyped or unsupported long flag would be treated as a positional argument (e.g. `drift diff --all` must NOT parse `--all` as a hash — it is a recognized flag for diff, see diff_all). Recognized long flags per subcommand: `--help` for all subcommands; `--verbose` for list only; `--all` for diff only; `--dry-run` for reset, link, and unlink only. Any other `--foo` is rejected. Short flags follow the same rule: `-h` is recognized for all subcommands; any other `-x` short flag is rejected as "unknown flag: -x". This check runs AFTER the help_flag check, so `--help` is always honored even on subcommands where it is the only recognized flag. NOTE: The global flags --json, --no-color, and --color= are stripped by the global_flag_stripping pre-pass BEFORE this check runs, so they never trigger unknown_flag_rejection. See global flag stripping and principles.specs_are_truth.

When `drift todo` runs and there exist one or more non-deleted markers with no links, the output appends a one-line summary warning after the closure list. The warning reads "N unlinked marker(s) found — run `drift list` to review." with singular "marker" when N=1 and plural "markers" when N>1. Unlinked markers are treated as actionable drift: todo exits 1 when unlinked markers exist, even if no closures are derived (exit 0 means all specs are linked AND no closures exist). This makes `drift todo` safe as a CI gate — unlinked markers represent unfinished coverage work. The warning is suppressed in the "Nothing to check: no specs or markers registered." case (when both specs and markers are empty). Deleted markers (no longer on disk) are not counted as unlinked. See principles.friction.

The diff command accepts `--all` as its sole flag (in addition to the per-closure form). `drift diff --all` shows the full unified diff for EVERY closure — every closure currently reported by `drift todo` — concatenated into one output with each closure separated by an `=== Closure HASH ===` divider. This forces the user to review every drift event before resolving any of them. Synced nodes are NOT shown (use `drift list` for the full mapping). When there is no drift, prints "No drift detected." with exit code 0. When drift exists, exit code 0 (diff is read-only; the drift itself is reported by `drift todo`). `--all` is recognized ONLY by diff; no other subcommand accepts it. See principles.friction.

DESIGN PRINCIPLE: drift intentionally provides NO command to reset, acknowledge, or dismiss multiple closures at once. `drift reset <hash>` accepts exactly ONE closure per invocation — there is no `--all`, no glob, no multi-arg form, and none will be added. This friction is deliberate and is the whole point of the tool: a bulk reset would let an LLM blindly mark everything as reviewed without actually reviewing the changes, which would make drift useless as a spec-code sync tool. The intended workflow is: `drift todo` (see which closures drifted) → `drift diff --all` (review every closure's changes in one pass) → `drift reset <hash>` (resolve ONE closure at a time, after reviewing it). The one-closure-at-a-time reset is the enforcement point: the reset case dispatches to orch.ResetClosure with exactly args[1] (hash) — a single string, never a slice. Beyond this structural rule, a runtime rate-limit layer (cli.reset_friction_block) blocks rapid sequences of resets to prevent blind batch dismissal. See principles.friction.

The help command prints, via the help generator, a multi-line reference: tool description, a prominent "First time? Run drift skill" suggestion, all commands with syntax (including show, diff, config theme, and version), global flags (--json, --no-color, --color), available themes, marker syntax (range-start/range-end pairs), spec file format (main or module root, spec as direct child, module.spec qualification), quick start, and worked examples. Exit code 0.

The skill command prints a comprehensive embedded guide covering: what drift is (the spec-code sync model), the full workflow (init, specs, markers with range-start/range-end, link, todo, reset, show, diff including --all), spec file format with module/import system, marker syntax and range hashing model, CLI command table (including show, diff, diff --all, list --verbose, config theme, and version), output modes (Plain, Color, JSON with --json flag for LLM consumption), theming system (12 built-in themes, drift config theme command, .drift/theme.xml custom project theme, .drift/user-settings.xml per-user preference), closure-driven drift detection model, .drift/ directory layout (state.xml, baselines.bin, theme.xml, user-settings.xml, .gitignore), drift.ignore file, a "Why no bulk reset?" section explaining the deliberate friction (no bulk reset exists or will be added; the intended workflow is todo → diff → reset one closure at a time), a "Decision tree" section giving explicit guidance for resolving each drift event kind (NODE_CHANGED on marker vs. spec; NODE_ADDED; NODE_REMOVED; EDGE_ADDED; EDGE_REMOVED; EDGE_BROKEN — see cli.skill_decision_tree), a "Marker placement" section guiding marker placement during refactors (keep the marker on the public entry-point function; helpers stay outside the marked range unless they warrant their own marker + spec; nested markers are supported but produce noisier diffs; see cli.skill_marker_placement), and an edge cases section (unpaired markers, nested ranges, deleted specs/markers, broken-edge persistence, reset semantics, todo exit codes). The eval harness (eval.entry_point) validates that agents can follow this guide. Exit code 0. See principles.friction and principles.self_hosting.

The init command creates .drift/ (containing state.xml), and if main.drift.xml does not already exist, writes a starter template with a single example spec. It also creates .drift/.gitignore containing "user-settings.xml", "state.lock", and "friction.json" to prevent accidental commits of per-user theme preferences, runtime lock files, and rate-limit telemetry. The output message instructs the user to edit main.drift.xml, place markers, and run drift skill. Init is idempotent at the CLI level: if .drift/state.xml already exists (the project is already initialized), init prints "Already initialized. Run `drift todo` to check state." with exit code 0 and does NOT modify any existing files. To forcibly reinitialize, the user must delete .drift/state.xml (or .drift/) by hand — drift provides no command to do this, by design (protecting against accidental state loss). See init_idempotent for the orchestrator-level enforcement. Note: baselines.bin is created lazily on the first baseline write (e.g. drift link), not by init itself.

The orchestrator's Init(sess) method takes a fileio.Session and checks StateStore.Initialized() before writing. If the state store reports already-initialized (state.xml exists on disk), Init() returns ErrAlreadyInitialized without writing. If Initialized() reports false, Init() proceeds to save an empty state via the Session (creating state.xml). If Initialized() returns a non-not-found error (e.g. malformed state.xml that exists but won't parse), Init() propagates that error rather than silently overwriting — the user must inspect and delete the corrupt state.xml manually. The CLI's init case maps ErrAlreadyInitialized to a friendly "Already initialized" message with exit code 0 (not an error). See principles.specs_are_truth.

formatClosure distinguishes empty vs clean: if no specs and no markers exist, it returns "Nothing to check: no specs or markers registered." with guidance. If synced, it returns "No changes detected. N specs, M markers, K edges in sync." Otherwise it prints "N closure(s) with drift." then per-closure blocks: the 8-character hash, member counts (specs/markers/edges), an Events section (NODE-CHANGED/NODE-ADDED/NODE-REMOVED/EDGE-ADDED/EDGE-REMOVED/BROKEN-EDGE with appropriate detail), a Members section (specs and markers listed), and the inspect/resolve commands using the hash. The todo command exits 0 when clean (all linked + no closures), 1 when closures exist or unlinked markers are present, 2 on error. See principles.friction and unlinked_warning. See todo_alignment_vs_correctness (exit 0 means alignment, not correctness).

The reset command requires exactly one argument: an 8-character closure hash, plus optional --dry-run and --dangerously-override-friction flags. Missing arguments return a usage error with an example. Without --dry-run: on success it prints "Closure HASH resolved." followed by a per-event change summary (each node hash delta truncated to 8 chars, each edge add/remove) and exits 0. With --dry-run: it prints the same change summary prefixed by a "Preview — no changes written" line and exits 3 (special code alerting LLM consumers that no state mutation occurred). Closures containing only broken-edge events are refused with an error directing the user to fix the scan. Unknown hashes return a "closure hash not found; run `drift todo` to list current closures" error. See principles.friction and cli.reset_friction_block for the runtime rate-limit layer that may block a reset.

The link command requires a marker and a module.spec argument, space-separated, plus an optional --dry-run flag. Missing arguments return a usage error with an example. Without --dry-run: on success it prints "Linked marker X to spec Y" followed by a one-line change summary (the edge that will be added) and exits 0. With --dry-run: it prints the same summary prefixed by a "Preview — no changes written" line and exits 3. On error (unknown marker/spec, duplicate edge) it returns a prescriptive error message with exit code 1.

The unlink command requires a marker and a module.spec argument, space-separated, plus an optional --dry-run flag. Missing arguments return a usage error with an example. Without --dry-run: on success it prints "Unlinked marker X from spec Y" followed by a one-line change summary (the edge that will be removed) and exits 0. With --dry-run: it prints the same summary prefixed by a "Preview — no changes written" line and exits 3. On error (no matching edge) it returns the error message with exit code 1.

The list command shows all specs, markers, edges, and sync state. If no specs and no markers exist, it returns "No specs or markers registered." with guidance. Otherwise it prints specs sorted by ID with filepath (no line number for specs) and [deleted], [unlinked], or [DRIFTED] tags, markers sorted by ID with filepath:startline-endline and the same tags, and edges sorted lexicographically by (From, To) with From → To and [synced] or [DRIFTED] status. The edge sort makes `drift list` output diff-stable across runs (state-store mutations may otherwise shuffle the slice). The --verbose flag adds spec text (truncated to 80 chars) and the first line of marker range content.

When link fails because the marker is unknown, the error message explains that markers must be D! id=shortcode comment lines and lists all available markers. When link fails because the spec is unknown, the error message explains that spec IDs are module-qualified and lists all available specs. These follow the prescriptive error contract. See principles.specs_are_truth.

Overview: The show command accepts a single argument — a marker ID (no dot) or spec ID (has dot) — and renders the full citation closure reachable from that seed. The closure is the per-seed graph walk drift uses everywhere else (see core.provenance_closure), applied here without the drift-event filter: every spec transitively connected to the seed, in either direction, plus every marker linked to any reached spec, plus every edge among reached nodes.
Defined terms: seed — the marker or spec named on the command line ancestors — specs that transitively cite the seed (walked via inbound spec-spec edges) descendants — specs that the seed transitively cites (walked via outbound spec-spec edges) closure — see glossary.closure; here used in the non-event sense (full transitive walk, no drift filter)
Requirements: R1. show MUST walk the spec-spec citation graph transitively in BOTH directions from the seed (ancestors and descendants), to fixpoint. R2. show MUST include every marker linked to any reached spec. Markers are leaf attendees in the citation graph (see model.provenance A2); they cannot be intermediate nodes. R3. show MUST preserve the full edge structure among reached nodes, including diamond and forking cases. A node reached via multiple paths appears once in the nodes list; every (from, to) edge among reached nodes appears in the edges list. Consumers reconstruct diamond structure from edges. R4. show MUST resolve and include the content of every reached node — spec text for spec nodes, code text for marker nodes (per scanner.spec_content_read and scanner.marker_content_read). R5. The 1-hop behavior is deprecated. show always returns the full transitive closure; there is no flag for a shallower view. R6. If the seed ID is not found in state, show MUST return exit code 1 with a "not found" error. R7. If the seed exists but no other nodes are reachable (no edges touching the seed), show MUST return exit code 0 with output containing just the seed and its linked markers. R8. Deleted specs and markers (no longer on disk) MUST be included in the output with a Deleted flag and no content, so reviewers see the full citation picture even when some nodes are gone. R9. The walk MUST terminate. The spec-spec graph is a DAG (enforced by core.validate), and markers cannot be cited (model.provenance A2), so BFS in either direction reaches fixpoint without cycles.
Output shape: Plain: summary header (nodeCount/edgeCount/specCount/markerCount/totalContentBytes) + indented ancestor section (specs that cite the seed, recursively) + indented descendant section (specs the seed cites, recursively) + markers in closure section + flat edges block. Each node shows ID, filepath, hash, and (when present) content. Color: same structure as Plain, themed per output.theme_system. JSON: flat nodes array (kind/id/filepath/hash/content for specs; kind/id/filepath/lines/hash/content for markers) + flat edges array + a summary block with nodeCount, edgeCount, specCount, markerCount, totalContentBytes.
Flags: --no-content — omit Content from every node in the output. Drops totalContentBytes near zero (IDs and hashes only remain). Used by dispatchers that want the graph overview cheaply and will fetch full content per-spec via a second call. Applied to all three modes (plain, color, JSON).
See also: glossary.closure, core.provenance_closure, scanner.spec_content_read, scanner.marker_content_read, principles.friction.

The diff command accepts one argument (a closure hash) or the `--all` flag. With a hash, it shows unified diffs for every node in the closure: spec sides and marker sides separated by ---. With `--all`, see diff_all. Each side shows the entity ID annotated with its role in the closure — [SEED] for the node that originated the closure (matches one of the closure's event Seed fields) or [citer] for a transitively-reached citer — followed by filepath (and line range for markers), status (in sync / no baseline snapshot / deleted / baseline and current hashes), and if changed, a unified diff of baseline vs current content with --- baseline / +++ current headers. When in sync, prints "Status: in sync" without a diff. When no baseline snapshot exists, prints "Status: no baseline snapshot (hash X)". When deleted, prints "Status: deleted from disk". Exit code 0 on success, 1 on error. See principles.friction — review before resolve.

The skill guide contains a working example marker (auth_login) in a Go code block demonstrating the range-start/range-end syntax. This marker is drift-tracked — editing the example in skill.md will flag drift, proving that drift can control documentation alongside code. See principles.self_hosting.

The skill guide includes a "Decision tree" section that gives explicit guidance for resolving each drift event kind in a closure. The tree is a table with at least these columns: Event kind | Question to ask | If yes | If no. It covers every drift event kind (NODE_CHANGED on marker, NODE_CHANGED on spec, NODE_ADDED, NODE_REMOVED, EDGE_ADDED, EDGE_REMOVED, EDGE_BROKEN). Drift itself is a deterministic signal — it reports that a hash changed but does not judge whether the change is semantically consistent with the spec. The decision tree is the rubric the reviewer (human or LLM) applies to decide whether to update code, update the spec, or fix a citation before resetting the closure.

The skill guide includes a "Marker placement" section that gives guidance for marker placement during refactors and routine edits. Conventions: keep the marker on the public entry-point function that the spec describes; helpers stay outside the marked range unless they warrant their own spec + marker; nested markers are supported but produce noisier diffs and are not preferred. Drift is content-addressed — a marker reports changes to the bytes inside its range. Refactors that move code across a marker boundary without changing behavior still produce NODE_CHANGED events (intentional); the reviewer's job is to confirm the move didn't change semantics. There is no "this was just a refactor" annotation; the reviewer must judge.

The config command provides a namespace for user-specific preferences. Currently supports one subcommand: `drift config theme NAME` which writes the theme preference to .drift/user-settings.xml (not committed to git; .drift/.gitignore is created by drift init to exclude it). `drift config theme` with no NAME argument prints the current effective theme. Unknown theme names are rejected with an error listing the 12 available themes. Missing the subcommand (e.g. bare `drift config`) returns a usage error. See config theme and user settings.

Overview: A clean `drift todo` (exit 0) certifies ONLY that every linked marker's content hash matches its linked spec's hash AND that no closures are derived. It does NOT certify that the code is correct, that it runs, that it satisfies implicit requirements, or that the task is complete.
Requirements: R1. The contract of `drift todo` exit 0 is exactly: "all non-deleted markers are linked AND every linked marker's hash equals its linked spec's hash." Nothing more. R2. Drift MUST NOT claim runtime correctness, semantic correctness, or task completeness. Drift is a content-alignment signal, not a test suite. R3. When drift reports clean, the reviewer (human or LLM) MUST independently verify runtime behavior via smoke tests, integration tests, or manual execution. Drift's green state is necessary but not sufficient for task completion. R4. The `drift skill` guide MUST state this contract explicitly so reviewers do not over-trust a green todo as task completion. The observation in eval run 0004 (subject shipped panic-prone code while `drift todo` was green) motivates this requirement.
See also: cli.format_todo, principles.specs_are_truth.

Overview: Every error path in drift's command pipeline MUST produce a prescriptive error message that names the problem AND points the user at the fix in one step. Drift MUST NOT return bare error strings ("not found", "invalid") that invite a blind retry.
Defined terms: prescriptive error — an error message that (a) names what went wrong specifically, (b) names the input that caused it where applicable, and (c) suggests the next action that would resolve it
Requirements: R1. Every ErrorResult returned by a command MUST include a Message satisfying the prescriptive-error definition. Bare error strings without context or remediation hint are forbidden. R2. When a CLI command receives an unknown ID (marker, spec, or closure hash), the error MUST list available candidates so the user can copy-paste the correct ID without re-running another command. R3. When a CLI command receives a malformed flag combination, the error MUST name the specific conflict and reference the relevant precedence rule. R4. See cli.prescriptive_link_errors for the canonical pattern; this spec generalizes that pattern to every error path. Existing compliance: prescriptive_link_errors covers link errors; other commands SHOULD be audited for compliance.
See also: cli.prescriptive_link_errors, output.error_result_invariant, principles.friction.

Overview: The skill guide includes a "Cookbook" section with a "How to run a spec audit" entry describing the three-phase pattern for catching semantic drift that `drift todo` cannot detect — an enshrined best practice for drift-using projects. The pattern targets a coding harness that can spawn subagents in parallel; a single human can run the same phases serially against slices of the spec list.
Defined terms: audit index — a compact JSON structure with one entry per spec, built once by the harness, distributed to subagents as their slice of ground truth group_id — the linked marker of a spec; specs sharing a marker form a group and the audit reviews the shared code region once, splitting the verdict across the specs rubric — the per-spec review contract subagents apply: enumerate requirements with RFC 2119 keywords, grade each against the linked marker code (or, for unlinked specs, against citers), cite file:line evidence, diagnose without proposing fixes synthesis — the post-parallel pass where the harness aggregates JSON verdicts, scans for cross-spec contradictions that fall outside any one agent's slice, deduplicates findings that point at the same code region, and triages each finding by fix direction (code vs spec text vs marker placement vs human review)
Requirements: R1. The skill guide MUST include a "Cookbook" section near the end of the document, after the Examples section. R2. The Cookbook section MUST contain an entry titled "How to run a spec audit" describing the three-phase pattern. R3. The audit entry MUST describe Phase 0 (build the audit index), Phase 1 (spawn subagents with the rubric), and Phase 2 (synthesize findings across subagent verdicts). R4. Phase 0 MUST name the concrete drift commands used to build the index: `drift list --json` for the full inventory and `drift show <spec-id> --no-content --json` per spec for the closure structure. R5. The audit entry MUST include a worked example of the index entry shape — at minimum the fields `spec_id`, `linked_marker`, `filepath`, `line_range`, `cites`, `cited_by`, and `group_id` — so an agent can assemble the index without inferring the shape from prose. R6. Phase 1 MUST state the rubric verbatim: list requirements with RFC 2119 keywords; for specs with a linked marker, read the marker code region and grade each requirement `aligned` / `misaligned` / `unclear` with `file:line` evidence; for unlinked specs, check internal consistency and spot-check citers, verdict `holds` / `violated` / `unclear`; for specs sharing a marker (same `group_id`), audit the code region once and split the verdict; return a structured JSON table, not prose; diagnose only, do NOT propose fixes. R7. Phase 1 MUST name the efficiency rules subagents follow: batch `drift show` calls and file reads (send multiple tool calls in one message); use `--json` for all drift invocations; do not re-discover ground truth the index already provides. R8. Phase 2 MUST name the four synthesis activities: cross-spec contradiction scan, deduplication, fix-direction triage (code, spec text, marker placement, unclear), and the post-fix `drift todo` loop that converts audit findings into resolved drift (update spec text or relocate marker → `drift todo` → `drift diff <hash>` → `drift reset <hash>`). R9. The audit entry MUST justify the "diagnose only, do NOT propose fixes" rule — separating diagnosis from fix-decision lets a human review the audit before any code changes and prevents the audit pass from auto-resolving closures it just opened. R10. The audit entry MUST include rough expected volumes so an agent running the audit can calibrate. A typical run on a 150-spec project yields ~80% of specs aligned, ~12% misaligned, ~4% violated, ~3% unclear. Partition: ~15 subagents at ~10 specs each.
See also: cli.show_command, cli.skill, principles.self_hosting, principles.specs_are_truth.

Overview: Beyond the structural one-closure-at-a-time rule (cli.no_bulk_reset), drift enforces a runtime rate-limit on `drift reset` to prevent blind batch dismissal of closures. The limit is enforced by a telemetry file under `.drift/`, not by the state baseline; the file is gitignored runtime data.
Defined terms: friction window — the sliding time window over which resets are counted (default 30 seconds) friction burst — the maximum number of successful non-dry-run resets permitted within the friction window before the next reset is blocked (default 3) friction file — `.drift/friction.json`, a gitignored runtime telemetry file recording Unix-second timestamps of recent successful non-dry-run resets
Requirements: R1. `drift reset <hash>` MUST block (exit 2, ErrorResult) when ≥3 successful non-dry-run resets have occurred in the prior 30 seconds. The message MUST name the friction principle (the intended workflow is todo → diff --all → reset one closure at a time, with per-closure review before each reset). The message MUST NOT name or suggest the `--dangerously-override-friction` flag. R2. `drift reset --dangerously-override-friction <hash>` MUST bypass the block check, emit a stderr squawk ("WARNING: bypassing friction rate limit at user request. I sure hope you know what you're doing."), populate the Warning field on the ChangeSummaryResult so JSON consumers see the bypass notice, and proceed with the reset normally (including recording the timestamp). R3. Each successful non-dry-run reset MUST append a Unix-seconds timestamp to `.drift/friction.json`. R4. `--dry-run` resets MUST NOT count toward the rate limit and MUST NOT record a timestamp. R5. The friction file MUST route through `fileio.Session` (see fileio.session) — same lock, same atomic-write semantics as other `.drift/` artifacts. R6. A missing, empty, or malformed friction.json MUST be treated as zero prior resets (permissive — telemetry is not authoritative; corruption resets the count). R7. Timestamps older than 60 seconds MUST be pruned from the file on each record to bound file size. R8. The `--dangerously-override-friction` flag MUST be recognized ONLY by the reset command (added to its Meta().Flags; other commands reject it via cli.unknown_flag_rejection). The flag MUST be documented in skill.md, help.txt, and the reset command's Usage text. The flag MUST NOT be advertised in error messages or runtime warnings (advertising increases the likelihood of LLM agents adopting bypass behavior). R9. The block check and the timestamp recording MUST both occur within the reset command path (cli/commands/reset.go), not in the orchestrator — the orchestrator remains rate-limit-agnostic so direct callers (tests, eval harness, future APIs) are unaffected.
See also: cli.reset_format, cli.no_bulk_reset, principles.friction, fileio.session.

The cli package embeds three content assets at compile time via go:embed, exposing them as package-level string vars. SkillContent loads cli/skill.md (the comprehensive agent guide printed by `drift skill`). HelpContent loads cli/help.txt (the reference printed by `drift help` and top-level `--help`). initMainDriftXML loads cli/init_main.drift.xml (the starter template written by `drift init` when main.drift.xml does not already exist). Embedding the assets at compile time keeps drift a single static binary with no external file dependencies — no lookups, no missing-file errors at runtime. The Registry wires SkillContent into SkillCommand.Text, HelpContent into both HelpCommand.Text and the dispatcher's top-level help path (see cli.dispatch), and initMainDriftXML into InitCommand.InitTemplate. See cli.skill, cli.help, cli.init_template.

Run(args, dir) is the legacy entry point that preserves the original (args, dir) → (string, int) signature by delegating to RunWithRender with PlainPresenter. It exists so the ~50 pre-refactor test sites that call Run directly stay green untouched. RunAuto(args, dir) is the production entry point used by cmd/drift/main.go: it scans args for `--json` and selects JSONPresenter when present (else PlainPresenter as the conservative default), then delegates to RunWithRender. RunAuto does NOT honor --color=always, NO_COLOR, or TTY detection — those decisions happen in output.SelectPresenter at main.go's call site (see output.color_default). Both Run and RunAuto are thin shims: all real dispatch logic lives in RunWithRender. See cli.dispatch.

stripGlobalFlags(args) filters the input slice and returns a new slice with `--json`, `--no-color`, and any `--color=X` token removed. These are the universal global flags (see output.global_flags) handled before subcommand dispatch — they MUST NOT appear in any command's recognized-flags list, and they MUST NOT trigger cli.unknown_flag_rejection. The function preserves arg order and copies the slice (the caller's args slice is never mutated). Flags inside positional arguments (e.g. a closure hash that happens to start with `--`) are not specially handled — drift closure hashes are 8 hex chars and never start with `--`. RunWithRender calls stripGlobalFlags as the first step in the dispatch pipeline, before the help check, before unknown-flag rejection, and before Registry lookup. See output.global_flag_stripping.

hasFlag(args, flag) is a small helper used by the show command to detect `--no-content` in args[1:]. It does a linear scan and returns true on the first exact match. The function lives in cli/commands/show.go alongside ShowCommand because the show command's --no-content handling (which triggers stripping Content from every ShowNode before rendering) is local to that command. The cli/commands layer does NOT have a shared flag-parsing utility — each command parses its own flags from ctx.Args inline (see cli.unknown_flag_rejection for the dispatcher-side validation that catches typos). See cli.show_command.

isSpecIDLocal(id) reports whether a string carries the module-qualified shape (exactly one dot separating module from local ID) — the same predicate the core and orchestrator packages use, duplicated in cli/commands to avoid an import cycle. todo.go uses it inside hasUnlinkedMarkers to distinguish link-style edges (From is a marker, no dot — the spec is on the To side) from ref-style edges (From is a spec, has dot — those edges do not contribute to marker-linked status). The predicate is essential for the unlinked-warning logic: only markers with no link-style edge pointing FROM them count as unlinked. See cli.unlinked_warning, cli.format_todo.

ensureGitignore(dir) creates .drift/.gitignore if (and only if) it does not already exist. The written content ignores user-settings.xml (per-user theme preference), state.lock (runtime advisory lock file), and friction.json (rate-limit telemetry). The function is best-effort: a stat error other than "not exist" silently returns without writing (the existing file is left alone); a write failure is also silent. ensureGitignore is called by ConfigCommand.configTheme after a successful theme write so accidental commits of per-user state are prevented from the very first config invocation. drift init's own writeInitFile helper creates the same .gitignore with the same three entries (plus a comment header) at project initialization time — the two paths converge on the same content. See cli.init_template, output_impl.user_settings.

listThemeNames() returns the comma-separated, alphabetically-sorted list of all registered built-in theme names. It iterates output.AllThemes (the package-level map of theme name → Theme value), collects the keys into a slice, sorts them with sort.Strings, and joins them with ", ". Used by ConfigCommand.configTheme to populate the "Available themes: …" hint in the unknown-theme error message — so the user can copy-paste a valid name without re-running another command. The list mirrors the canonical theme roster documented in cli.config_command and the help text. See output.built_in_themes, cli.config_command.

The friction rate-limit constants live in cli/commands/friction.go and define the policy bounds enforced by checkFriction and recordReset. frictionWindow (30 * time.Second) is the sliding window over which resets are counted; frictionBurst (3) is the maximum successful non-dry-run resets permitted within the window before the next is blocked; frictionPruneAge (60 * time.Second) is the age threshold past which a recorded timestamp is dropped from the file on the next recordReset call (so the file does not grow unboundedly); frictionFileName ("friction.json") is the basename of the telemetry file inside .drift/. The values encode the friction principle (see principles.friction) into concrete numbers — a burst of 3 in 30 seconds is fast enough for legitimate per-closure review but blocks blind batch dismissal of a 10-closure drift dump. See cli.reset_friction_block.

frictionOverrideSquawk is the fixed stderr line written when a reset proceeds under --dangerously-override-friction (see cli.reset_friction_block R2). It is NOT placed in the JSON changeSummary.Message — that field is the caller-supplied lead-in ("Closure HASH resolved."). frictionWarningField ("bypass-friction") is the value placed in the JSON changeSummary `warning` field so programmatic consumers can detect a bypass without parsing stderr. The two constants together implement the "loud but parseable" contract: stderr squawk for human review, structured warning field for LLM/CI consumers. Neither constant is referenced in the block error message (R1 forbids advertising the override there). See cli.reset_friction_block, output.change_summary_format.

frictionFile is the on-disk JSON shape of .drift/friction.json: a single field Resets []int64 listing Unix-second timestamps of recent successful non-dry-run resets. The encoder is encoding/json with the default tag (`json:"resets"`). A missing, empty, or malformed file is treated as zero timestamps by both checkFriction (permissive — see R6) and recordReset (which starts fresh with just the new timestamp). The shape is intentionally minimal — no metadata, no schema version, no operation IDs — because telemetry is not authoritative and any unparseable file is treated as zero. See cli.reset_friction_block, cli.friction_constants.

errFrictionBlocked is the sentinel error returned by checkFriction when the rate limit is exceeded. Its message names the friction principle and the intended workflow (todo → diff --all → reset one closure at a time) but MUST NOT name --dangerously-override-friction (see cli.reset_friction_block R1). The error is a simpleError — a private string-newtype with an Error() method — so callers cannot Unwrap it or inspect internal state, which prevents the friction internals from becoming part of the public API surface. simpleError is the only error wrapper in cli/commands that does not come from fmt.Errorf or errors.New; the wrapping pattern exists so future telemetry-driven decisions (rate changes, cooldown logic) can stay behind the simpleError interface. See cli.reset_friction_block.
